author.name: Department of Materials at ETH Zurich

media:group.media:title: Materials Day 2013 - Talk "Synthetic 2D Polymers" of Prof. A. Dieter Schlüter
media:group.media:description:
Talk from 13.11.2013
The Symposium “Materials Day” is organized biannually by the Department of Materials at ETH Zurich to bring together faculty, researchers and students with representatives from industry and the media. The “Materials Day” offers scientific information and opportunities for interaction among the materials community. It is organized as a full day symposium including oral presentations and poster sessions. The 2013 Materials Day “Department of Materials – Today, Tomorrow and Beyond” aims to give a comprehensive overview over the groups that make up the Department of Materials with a clear focus on future research directions.
Video from ETH Video Portal.

entry.title: Materialwissenschaft – Römischer Beton im Wissensmagazin SRF Einstein

author.name: Department of Materials at ETH Zurich

media:group.media:title: Materialwissenschaft – Römischer Beton im Wissensmagazin SRF Einstein
media:group.media:description:
Ausschnitt aus dem SRF Einstein Beitrag vom 18.11.2021, SRF 1, Titel "Baden wie die Römer".
Das Forschungsteam von Prof. Caseri am Departement Materialwissenschaft, ETH Zürich hat den römischen Beton aus Baden untersucht und herausgefunden, dass dieser Beton anders zusammengesetzt ist als der bislang bekannte römische Beton. Was genau der Unterschied ist und warum sich nun auch die Industrie für die «römische» Technologie interessiert? Dies und vieles mehr gibt es im Video zu erfahren!
https://www.srf.ch/play/tv/einstein/video/baden-wie-die-roemer?urn=urn:srf:video:221204b1-7b71-4ec9-bafe-1cc0c9b10f70 Video von SRF Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen, SRF Einstein (Urheber)
Laboratory for Multifunctional Materials, Department of Materials, ETH Zurich https://multimat.mat.ethz.ch
Sprache: Deutsch und Schweizerdeutsch Untertitel: Deutsch

entry.title: sallea - From the academic idea to an industrial product

author.name: Department of Materials at ETH Zurich

media:group.media:title: sallea - From the academic idea to an industrial product
media:group.media:description:
3D printing has led to a paradigm shift in the world of design. But many high performance materials are incompatible with printing. Water-soluble, printed salt templates give these materials, like magnesium, access to complex lattice structures with the potential to heal bone, make lighter space shuttles and efficient cooling systems.
Der 3D-Druck hat zu einem Paradigmenwechsel in der Welt des Designs geführt. Doch viele Hochleistungsmaterialien sind noch immer nicht direkt druckbar. Wasserlösliche, gedruckte Gussformen aus Salz geben solchen Materialien, wie zum Beispiel Magnesium, Zugang zu komplexen Gitterstrukturen. Diese haben so das Potenzial, Knochen zu heilen, leichtere Raumfähren zu ermöglichen oder Kühlsysteme noch effizienter zu gestalten.
Video from N. Kleger & S. Fehlmann, sallea®

entry.title: Would you rather have glass or this noiseless extra tough material in your windows?

author.name: Department of Materials at ETH Zurich

media:group.media:title: Would you rather have glass or this noiseless extra tough material in your windows?
media:group.media:description:
Imagine you have to design the wing of an airplane, or the frame of a bicycle. You would need a material that is strong, but yet able to absorb vibrations. These two properties are incompatible in nature and materials that combine them are scarce, which leads to a materials selection dilemma. A special design approach allows researchers at LNM to overcome this dilemma. In the video we show how a new composite that is both strong and efficient at damping vibration compares with typical glass. It is also transparent but no, transparent planes or bikes are a long way to go!
Reference to ETH D-MATL, Laboratory for Nanometallurgy: https://met.mat.ethz.ch and the article https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0266353821001007

media:group.media:title: The Next Step for 3D Printing
media:group.media:description: 3D printing of Liquid crystal polymer (LCP) into high-performance polymer structures with mechanical properties that surpass all other available printable polymers and can compete even with fibre-reinforced composites. These properties result from the molecular alignment that can be generated during the printing process of LCPs and that can be tailored locally to optimize the mechanical response of complex geometries.
